description:
Astra Vitae is an interdisciplinary team exploring how technology can help protect human health in space. We combine software development and medical expertise to create practical, thoughtful solutions.

We're looking for curious people who enjoy learning and building together, with interests in AI, data science, biomedical engineering, or space exploration. Whatever your background, enthusiasm and a willingness to contribute matter most.

Let's build something meaningful together.
summary:
Órbita is an offline-capable health monitoring prototype that helps astronauts understand their health and follow up on care activities during space missions. We developed a visual application combining personal health records, physical adaptation, habitat conditions, guided procedures, and a daily action plan.

Its “I feel different” workflow connects an observation with available measurements, information gaps, equipment requirements, and follow-up. Users can record symptoms and measurements, track tasks and results, and export records for medical review. Selected NASA ground-analog datasets provide research cases, kept separate from the fictional astronaut demonstration.

Órbita addresses the challenge by connecting health visualization with practical self-assessment and continuity of care. Missing data stays visible, while measurements retain their source and context. Guidance workflows use clearly labeled fictional content; clinical guidance requires qualified review.

Astronauts far from Earth need to understand what is known, what is missing, and what actions remain pending. Órbita aims to support greater autonomy and clearer communication when medical support is delayed.
details:
Órbita is a personal health companion designed to help astronauts turn health information into clear, connected actions. It brings together personal health, physical adaptation, and habitat conditions in one visual experience, supporting both daily routines and moments when something feels different.

The journey starts with a simple observation: “I feel different.” From there, users can review available measurements, identify missing information, follow a procedure, record what happened, and track the next step. A daily plan and shared timeline connect observations, activities, and results, while exportable summaries help prepare information for medical review.

What makes Órbita creative is this continuity. Beyond displaying metrics, it connects what the astronaut notices with the information and resources available during the mission. Selected NASA ground-analog datasets provide research cases, clearly separated from the fictional demonstration.

Built with web technologies, Órbita can run offline and keep records on the device. The team considered limited connectivity, equipment availability, ease of use, and the importance of showing uncertainty. Missing information stays visible, and every measurement retains its source and context.

Our intended impact is greater autonomy and clearer communication when Earth is far away. Órbita demonstrates how health monitoring can become an understandable, actionable part of mission life. The current prototype uses clearly labeled demonstration guidance; clinical guidance requires qualified review.
